# SPSC Ring Buffer for Low-Latency Communication

## Single Producer, Single Consumer (SPSC)

```
Use case: one thread produces, one thread consumes
Example: network RX thread → app processing thread

Traditional queue (mutex-based):
  ├─ Every operation takes a lock, even when uncontended
  ├─ Contention: the other thread blocks, or the OS parks it
  └─ Cost: lock handoff shows up in the tail, not the median

Lock-free SPSC ring buffer:
  ├─ No locks: each index has exactly one writer
  ├─ Circular array: fixed memory, allocated once up front
  ├─ Two atomic indices, no read-modify-write instructions
  └─ Cost: a few loads, one store, no syscalls
```

Absolute timings (nanoseconds per operation, mutex versus ring) depend on the machine, the compiler and the contention pattern. Quote them only from a captured run on named hardware: `pow run spsc -- <benchmark command>`. Typical "about 100 ns" and "about 1 to 5 µs" figures in older notes are [VERIFY] and are not repeated here.

The one-line pitch for an interview: **an SPSC queue is lock-free because every shared variable has exactly one writer.**

## The Buffer

A ring buffer is a fixed array treated as if its end were glued to its start. Two indices chase each other around it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ring[Ring of 4 slots]
        S0[slot 0] --> S1[slot 1] --> S2[slot 2] --> S3[slot 3] --> S0
    end
    C[consumer owns head: next slot to pop] -.-> S0
    P[producer owns tail: next slot to push] -.-> S2
```

In the picture, slots 0 and 1 hold items waiting to be popped, slots 2 and 3 are free. The consumer reads at `head`, the producer writes at `tail`. Neither ever writes the other's index.

Two conventions you must be able to state:

- **Empty**: `head == tail`.
- **Full**: `tail - head == N`, using free-running indices (below). The older "keep one slot empty" variant uses `(tail + 1) % N == head` and wastes a slot.

## Implementation

Use free-running indices that only ever increase, and mask them to find the slot. With `N` a power of two, `i & (N - 1)` equals `i % N` and avoids a division.

```cpp
template <class T, std::size_t N>
class SpscQueue {
    static_assert(N > 0 && (N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be a power of two");
    static constexpr std::size_t kMask = N - 1;

    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};  // written only by the consumer
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};  // written only by the producer
    alignas(64) std::array<T, N> buf_{};

public:
    bool try_push(const T& v) {                      // producer thread only
        const std::size_t t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        if (t - head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire) == N) return false;  // full
        buf_[t & kMask] = v;
        tail_.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_release);  // publish the item
        return true;
    }

    bool try_pop(T& out) {                           // consumer thread only
        const std::size_t h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        if (h == tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return false;      // empty
        out = buf_[h & kMask];
        head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release);  // hand the slot back
        return true;
    }
};
```

Design choices worth naming:

- Each side reads **its own** index with `relaxed` (nobody else writes it) and the **other** side's index with `acquire`.
- The indices never wrap to zero explicitly. Unsigned overflow of `std::size_t` is well defined, and because `N` divides 2^64, the subtraction `tail - head` stays correct across overflow.
- `head_` and `tail_` sit on separate cache lines (`alignas(64)`); see Scale.

## Worked Trace: Head and Tail Through Wraparound

Take `N = 4`, so `kMask = 3` (binary `11`). Start with `head = 0`, `tail = 0`. The slot is `index & 3`. Full means `tail - head == 4`.

| step | operation | check | slot | result | head | tail |
|------|-----------|-------|------|--------|------|------|
| 1 | push A | 0 - 0 = 0, not full | 0 & 3 = 0 | ok | 0 | 1 |
| 2 | push B | 1 - 0 = 1 | 1 & 3 = 1 | ok | 0 | 2 |
| 3 | push C | 2 - 0 = 2 | 2 & 3 = 2 | ok | 0 | 3 |
| 4 | push D | 3 - 0 = 3 | 3 & 3 = 3 | ok | 0 | 4 |
| 5 | push E | 4 - 0 = 4, full | none | rejected | 0 | 4 |
| 6 | pop | 0 != 4, not empty | 0 & 3 = 0 | returns A | 1 | 4 |
| 7 | pop | 1 != 4 | 1 & 3 = 1 | returns B | 2 | 4 |
| 8 | push E | 4 - 2 = 2, not full | 4 & 3 = 0 | ok, **wraps** | 2 | 5 |
| 9 | push F | 5 - 2 = 3 | 5 & 3 = 1 | ok | 2 | 6 |
| 10 | push G | 6 - 2 = 4, full | none | rejected | 2 | 6 |
| 11 | pop x4 | head 2, 3, 4, 5 | 2, 3, 0, 1 | returns C, D, E, F | 6 | 6 |
| 12 | pop | 6 == 6, empty | none | rejected | 6 | 6 |

What to notice:

- At step 8 the producer writes slot 0 again, but only because the consumer's pop at step 6 freed it. The producer learned that by reading `head`, never by taking a lock.
- Items come out in order A, B, C, D, E, F: FIFO holds across the wrap.
- `head` and `tail` keep growing (6 and 6 at the end) while the slot index cycles 0, 1, 2, 3. The *distance* `tail - head` is always between 0 and N, which is why the full and empty tests are unambiguous. With plain wrapped indices, `head == tail` would mean both empty and full, which is what the wasted slot in the older variant avoids.

## Why One Producer and One Consumer Need No Lock

A data race needs two threads touching the same location, at least one writing, without ordering between them. Walk through every shared location:

| location | writer | reader | safe because |
|----------|--------|--------|--------------|
| `tail_` | producer only | consumer | single writer; reader uses acquire |
| `head_` | consumer only | producer | single writer; reader uses acquire |
| `buf_[i]` | producer, while slot is free | consumer, once slot is published | the index hand-off orders the two accesses |

The key invariant: **a slot is owned by exactly one thread at any time.** Slots in `[head, tail)` belong to the consumer. Slots in `[tail, head + N)` belong to the producer. The producer moves a slot into the consumer's range by storing `tail` (release). The consumer moves it back by storing `head` (release). Ownership only changes through those two stores.

A stale read of the other side's index is harmless, only conservative:

- The producer sees an old `head`: it thinks the buffer is fuller than it is, and may reject a push that would have fit. It retries later.
- The consumer sees an old `tail`: it thinks the buffer is emptier than it is, and may report empty when an item has just arrived. It polls again.

Neither case corrupts data. This is also why the design breaks with a second producer: two threads would both write `tail_`, both could pick the same slot, and you would need a compare-and-swap loop or a lock. That is a different (MPSC or MPMC) queue.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant B as buf and indices
    participant C as Consumer
    P->>B: write item into buf at tail
    P->>B: store tail plus 1 with release
    C->>B: load tail with acquire
    Note over C,B: sees the new tail, so sees the item
    C->>B: read item from buf at head
    C->>B: store head plus 1 with release
    P->>B: load head with acquire
    Note over P,B: sees the freed slot, may reuse it
```

## Memory Ordering

```
Producer:
  write(buf[tail & mask])   ← must happen before
  release-store(tail)       ← consumer can now see the new tail

Consumer:
  acquire-load(tail)        ← synchronizes with producer's release
  read(buf[head & mask])    ← safe: producer's write is visible
```

The release store on `tail_` and the acquire load of it form a *synchronizes-with* edge in the C++ memory model: everything the producer wrote before the release is visible to the consumer after the acquire. The same pattern runs in reverse on `head_` so the producer never overwrites a slot the consumer is still reading.

Common mistakes:

- Using `relaxed` for the cross-thread loads and stores. The item write is then not ordered against the index update, and the consumer can read a half-written slot.
- Using `seq_cst` everywhere "to be safe". It is correct, but it can cost more than acquire/release on some architectures [VERIFY] (instruction-level differences vary by CPU; check the compiler's output for your target).
- Reading both indices with `acquire` on the thread that owns one of them. It is harmless but unnecessary; relaxed is enough for your own index because no other thread writes it.

On strongly ordered x86-64, acquire and release loads and stores usually compile to plain moves [VERIFY] (confirm with a disassembly of your build). On weakly ordered ARM they may emit extra instructions or special load/store forms [VERIFY]. Either way the source code must say acquire/release; relying on the hardware's strength is a bug waiting for a port.

## Scale

```
Capacity: N slots (power of two); usable capacity is N with free-running indices
Memory:   N * sizeof(T), contiguous, allocated once; no allocation on the hot path
Example:  1,048,576 slots of 256 bytes = 268,435,456 bytes (256 MiB) of buffer

Bottlenecks:
  ├─ Producer: copying T into the slot
  ├─ Consumer: copying T out of the slot
  ├─ Index cache-line ping-pong: each side must fetch the other's index
  └─ False sharing: head_ and tail_ on one cache line
```

**False sharing.** If `head_` and `tail_` share a cache line, every producer store invalidates the consumer's copy of the line and vice versa, even though they write different variables. Padding each index to its own line (64 bytes on many x86-64 and ARM parts [VERIFY] (check `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` or the CPU manual for your target)) removes that.

**Cached index optimisation.** Each side can keep a local copy of the other side's index and refresh it only when the cached value says full (producer) or empty (consumer). That cuts cross-core cache traffic on the common path. Treat it as an optimisation to measure, not to assume: capture a before and after with `pow run`.

**Batching.** Popping several items per acquire load amortises the index traffic when the consumer is behind.

---

## Interview Checklist

- [ ] SPSC: each index has exactly one writer, so no lock and no CAS
- [ ] Empty is `head == tail`; full is `tail - head == N` with free-running indices
- [ ] Power-of-two `N` so masking replaces modulo
- [ ] Release on the index store, acquire on the other side's index load
- [ ] Slot ownership: `[head, tail)` consumer, the rest producer
- [ ] Cache-line padding between `head_` and `tail_` to avoid false sharing
- [ ] Can trace a wraparound by hand (the table above)
- [ ] Say what breaks with two producers

## Common Wrong Answers

- ❌ "Use a mutex queue" — fine for correctness, but it puts lock handoff in the tail
- ❌ "Relaxed everywhere, it's only counters" — the item write is not ordered against the publish, so the consumer can read a torn slot
- ❌ "`head == tail` means full" — that is empty; full needs the distance or a spare slot
- ❌ "No padding needed, they're different variables" — separate variables on one cache line still false-share
- ❌ "Lock-free means it works with many producers" — the single-writer property is what you are relying on
